first_impression.reaction: Good, a straight answer in the first line, and it says where it came from, the government, not some blogger. That's what I wanted to know before we hand over any money: will this actually be a legal marriage back home. I'll read the rest properly, though I can already see a lot of Italian words I'll need explained.

journey.quote: Is marriage in Italy recognised in Australia? In most cases, yes: an overseas marriage is generally recognised here if it was valid where it took place and would have been valid under Australian law, according to both Smartraveller and the Attorney-General's Department.
journey.reaction: Thank you. A plain yes, and it names Smartraveller and the Attorney-General's Department. I trust that more than a glossy brochure.

journey.quote: You cannot register an Italian marriage in Australia, so bring home the comune's marriage certificate with a Prefettura apostille and have it translated in full.
journey.reaction: Comune, Prefettura, apostille, all in one sentence and none of them explained. I assume a comune is the town hall, but I shouldn't have to guess. My husband certainly won't know what an apostille is.

journey.section: Is an Italian marriage recognised in Australia?
journey.quote: Smartraveller suggests a lawyer confirm your certificate is valid here, which is worth doing if either of you was married before.
journey.reaction: Sensible. It doesn't pretend to be the lawyer. That's the sort of honest advice I like to see.

journey.section: When an Italian marriage would not be recognised
journey.quote: For most couples none of this applies. The one to check is an earlier divorce, which must be final before the Italian ceremony.
journey.reaction: The section numbers and the list about duress and fraud were heavy going, but this line settles it. Neither of them has been married, so we're fine.

journey.section: Make sure it is registered in Italy
journey.quote: Before you leave Italy, ask for the comune's certificate, not the parish's.
journey.reaction: Very practical, and exactly the kind of thing that would go wrong if nobody told you. Though again, if it's the town hall, just say town hall.

journey.quote: Book it for the first working days after the wedding.
journey.reaction: Book it who? My daughter, the day after her wedding, when she's meant to be on her honeymoon? Is she queuing at a government office in Italy by herself, or does someone do this for her? This is precisely the 'who is responsible' question I need answered.

journey.quote: Not published: Prefettura processing times. Ask your Wedded Advisor to build the appointment into your plan.
journey.reaction: The second half is reassuring, there's a person who will look after it. The 'Not published:' bit reads like a note someone forgot to delete. I had to read it twice.

journey.section: Travel in the name on your passport
journey.quote: Book the honeymoon in your current names and sort out the name change once home.
journey.reaction: Good, simple, and it saves a mess at the airport. I'll pass that one straight on.

journey.section: The trade-offs if Italy should be 'the' wedding
journey.quote: The cost is emotional. Your legal anniversary becomes a short ceremony at home, and some couples feel the Italian vows repeat something already done.
journey.reaction: I appreciate that it's honest about the downside rather than just selling. Doing the paperwork in Melbourne first sounds far simpler to me, but I can see my daughter feeling this way.

journey.section: The trade-offs if Italy should be 'the' wedding
journey.quote: Weigh whether to marry legally abroad or hold a symbolic ceremony before you put down a venue deposit.
journey.reaction: At last, the word deposit. Right advice, decide first, pay second. But it's the only mention, and it says nothing about whether that deposit is safe.

journey.quote: Can you divorce in Australia if you married in Italy?
journey.reaction: I know it's a fair legal question, but it's not something I want to read on a page I'm about to forward to the family about the wedding we're paying for.

journey.section: Get the legal side settled before you book
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor is one person from first idea to the last dance, working in your time zone and quoting in AUD, and confirms in writing what is included before you commit.
journey.reaction: This is what I want to hear: one person, Australian dollars, in writing. But who is this person? No name, no phone number, nothing on deposits or contracts with the Italian venue. Who do I ring if something goes wrong at 2am Italian time?

unanswered_questions: Who actually goes to the Prefettura for the apostille and arranges the translation: my daughter, or does the Wedded Advisor or someone in Italy do it for them?
Roughly what do the apostille and the NAATI translation cost, and how long does it all take before they can change her name?
Is the deposit protected? What happens to our money if the Italian venue or supplier lets us down?
Are the contracts with Italian venues in English and in AUD, and who is responsible if something goes wrong?
Who is the Wedded Advisor? Is there a named person and a phone number I can ring before anything is booked?
If they marry legally in Melbourne first, does Wedded Wonderland help organise that part too, or only the Italian day?

turn_offs_found.quote: Weigh whether to marry legally abroad or hold a symbolic ceremony before you put down a venue deposit.
turn_offs_found.why: The only mention of money changing hands, and nothing about who holds the deposit, whether it's protected, or who is accountable.

turn_offs_found.quote: You cannot register an Italian marriage in Australia, so bring home the comune's marriage certificate with a Prefettura apostille and have it translated in full.
turn_offs_found.why: Foreign and legal words with no plain-English explanation. I don't want to look old-fashioned asking what they mean.

would_share_with: My husband, with the deposit and 'who does the Prefettura appointment' questions written underneath
My daughter, the passport and honeymoon-names bit

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready, speak with a Wedded Advisor about which route suits you.
cta_reaction.why: 'Speak with' sounds like a phone call, which is what I want. But I'll talk it over with my husband first, and I'd click far more readily if it showed a name and a phone number rather than leaving me to guess whether it's a form.

top_3_changes: Explain the Italian and legal words in plain English the first time they appear (comune is the town hall, what the Prefettura is, what an apostille actually does).
Say plainly who handles the after-wedding Prefettura appointment and the translation, so I know my daughter isn't doing it alone on her honeymoon, and roughly what it costs and how long it takes.
In the closing section, tell me how I reach a real person by phone and what happens with deposits and contracts, since that's the bit I'm paying for.
